title: Krishna Sends Uddhava to Vrindavan
story:
In the palace at Mathura there were kings and counselors, kinsmen and crowds — but when Krishna wanted comfort carried to the people of his boyhood, he looked past them all. He looked to Uddhava, his dearest friend, whose heart was fixed on Krishna alone.

Uddhava held no office and no rank. What he had was rarer: he had been at Krishna's side through the long years in Mathura, and he had seen how Krishna, the young hero of the city, grew quiet whenever the talk turned to Vrindavan — how a single mention of the village could stop him mid-sentence. Krishna's heart was still there, among the cowherds who had raised him and the women who had loved him, and Uddhava knew it.

One day Krishna called Uddhava to him and gave him a journey. "Go to Vraja," he said — Vraja, the cowherd country of his childhood. "Bring joy to my parents." Nanda and Yashoda had raised him in the village of his boyhood; then the summons of the court of Kamsa — the cruel king of Mathura — had carried him away to the city, and the years since had been long for the people who still loved him there. But Krishna spoke of more than his parents.

"The women of Gokula," he told Uddhava, "have set their minds on me. Their very lives are given up for my sake; for my sake they have abandoned everything — comfort, standing, even their own bodies. To them I am the dearest of all dear ones, and I am far away. They are keeping themselves alive," he said, "with great difficulty — somehow, only just."

Uddhava understood what was being asked of him. Krishna was not sending a herald to deliver orders, or a prince to settle accounts. He was sending his own affection into the village that still sang his name — in the person of the one friend who could speak of him most truly. The women who had given up everything for Krishna were pining, and Krishna, who could have sent anyone, had chosen the one friend who would say the words the way they needed to be said. Uddhava accepted the charge: he would go to Vrindavan and tell Nanda and Yashoda of their son; he would carry Krishna's love to the women of Gokula; and he would not rest until he had done all that could be done to console them.

So he made ready to leave Mathura, carrying the strangest of royal messages: that Krishna, far away, remembered — remembered their songs and their meadows and their faces — and had sent the dearest of his friends to say so. He carried no army and no gifts, only words that would have to be worth the years of waiting. The road to Vrindavan lay open before him, and he set out.
reflection: The message Krishna entrusts to Uddhava is not doctrine but a description of love — minds fixed on him, lives given up for his sake. In sending his dearest friend to console Vrindavan, Krishna sends a part of himself, and comfort travels in both directions.
next_story_tease: He reached Vrindavan as the sun went down, to a welcome he had not expected.
hero_scene: In Mathura, Krishna sends his dearest devotee Uddhava on his way toward Vrindavan, one hand raised in farewell, while Uddhava turns toward the road that leads to the village of Krishna's childhood.
visual_elements: Krishna speaking with Uddhava, hand raised in farewell
Uddhava with a traveler's bundle, turning toward the road
the unseen village of Krishna's childhood beyond the horizon
